content.summary_of_the_paper:
In this paper the authors study the problem of computing a spectral clustering of a graph with duplicate edges that is partitioned across multiple sites, each holding a disjoint subset of the input graph. Similarly to other studies in the literature, both the message passing model and the blackboard model are considered. The authors are able to prove communication upper bounds for both models that are matching the known bounds on the non-duplication model which are optimal up to polylogarithmic factors, and achieve similar clustering quality guarantees.

The overall approach is to propagate between machines sparse subgraphs that retain the spectral properties of the subraphs on the different sites, and eventually run a centralized clustering algorithm on a sparse subraph that sumarizes the spectral properties of the whole graph. An additional challenge that arises in the duplication model is that one cannot simply compute independent sparsifiers on each site and unite all these subgraphs on the coordinator site to compute final clustering. The authors obtain their results via adapting the spectral sparsifier of Koutis & Xu (2016) to the distributed computation models that are considered in this study.  The Koutis-Xu sparsifier has two main components: 1) an adaptive construction of multiple spanners, and 2) an iterative edge sampling procedure (and re-weighing). The authors replace the adaptive spanner construction phase of the spectral sparsifier via bucketization of the edges based on their weights, and connections to known results that imply certain sparsity for graphs with large girth (a property that is ensured during the construction). To adapt the sampling procedure of the Koutis-Xu sparsifier, the authors introduce an assumption that each site knows the probability of any edge resides that the particular site. This allows them to perform the edge sampling adapted to the fact that there exist duplication in the set of edges. 

The authors also extensively study communication-efficient construction of spanners, under the blackboard model. Some of the results are not directly useful for the clustering objective, such as spanners with additive stretch, and small constant factor multiplicative stretch. For all these variants the authors provide upper and lower bounds.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
+ Communication upper bounds matching those of the non-duplicate model, for both models that are considered. These bounds are optimal up to polylogarithmic factors.
+ The presentation is excellent and easy to follow. Also the authors highlight well why some techniques fail to generalize to the duplication model.
+ An extensive study of graph spanners under the considered models, which could be of independent interest.

Weaknesses:
- The problem of clustering a graph with duplicate edges is not well motivated.
- The paper assumes that one knows the duplication factor of each edge, which is somehow artificial.
- The different results on spanner construction under the blackboard diverge from the topic of the paper.
- No experimental evaluation of the proposed method.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The presentation is excellent. The description of all the useful components is self-contained. In general, it was easy to go through the paper and understand the details.

The main technical contribution of the paper is the adaptation of the spanner construction that is needed for the Koutis-Xu spectral sparsifier, as the second main ingredient is somehow avoided via introducing the assumption on the knowledge of the duplication factor of each edge and on each site. The main spanner construction is proved via a clever combination of known (bucketization of edges, and show sparsity by ensuring large girth).
content.summary_of_the_review:
Overall, I liked reading the paper but hesitate recommending acceptance for the following reasons.

The motivation for studying this problem under the particular model is not clear to me. Is the duplication model something that people are concerned about? Does some other study provide some motivation? Currently, it seems that this is some setting where the existing techniques do not work. How unrealistic it would be to assume that duplicate edges appear on the same site?  This point also connects to the assumption that the authors make on the knowledge of the duplication factor of an edge, and across all sites. If making this information available across all sites, why doesn't one just gather all duplicate edges in a single machine and apply the previous approaches?

Some other notes:
At the current state of the paper, it is not clear why the authors study the different spanner constructions that are not directly needed for the main topic of the paper, which is the spectral-clustering objective. Even the study of the (2k-1) spanners seems a bit unrelated, as (4k-2) spanners suffice for the clustering results. It is unclear whether the lower bounds that the authors show have any implications for the clustering problem. On the positive side, these results could be of independent interest (although it would be hard for one to find those, as they are not the main topic of the study).

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This work presents distributed algorithms with limited communication for the problem of graph sparsification when the input graph is not necessarily *partitioned* across the machines.
- Prior work considers the case where each edge appears on exactly one machine, which makes it amenable to using the "composable coreset" idea, since *spectral* sparsifiers' definition is "linear".
- This work attempts to extend to the case where edges may appear on multiple machines. They use a limited definition though, where each edge is assigned probabilistically and uniformly to machines.
- The authors consider two models of communication: message-passing and blackboard. The proposed algorithm works with the data on each of the s machines in order one at a time. Therefore, the implementation in the message-passing framework essentially leads to O~(ns) bits of communication (with about n bits passed to the next machine when the processing is done for the current machine) while the blackboard model essentially allows O~(n+s) communication (as one only needs to output to the shared "blackboard" the incremental changes to the sparsifier/spanner being constructed). These bounds match (up to log factors) with known lower bounds and prior upper bounds for the case of no edge duplication (=edges partitioned initially on machines).
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
S1: Extends prior work to case where edges are not partitioned initially.
S2: Almost matches lower bounds & prior work's upper bounds in simpler cases.

W1: Paper's title "distributed clustering" is misleading. It's really about computing sparsifiers or spanners and then applying clustering on top of it. There are many notions of clustering and none is discussed here. It's assumed that a spectral sparsifier will be sufficient.
W2: The duplication model (random & uniform) is pretty weak. This appears only on Page 6, as if it is not a big restriction.
W3: Paper is hard to follow at times. Often times, terms or concepts are mentioned without defining them. Even the problem formulation is not clear unless one reads the theorems/proofs.
W4: Depending on the final title of the manuscript, several "related" works are missing. Distributed clustering results are not surveyed. On the spanner/sparsifier sider, too, there should be some overview of the best results in the non-distributed world. Decomposable coresets could be mentioned too.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The presentation needs quite a bit of improvement. Definitions (not necessarily very detailed) should appear first, so it becomes clear what is being discussed. See above.

There are several typos. Two examples:
- Page 4, before the last paragraph: "increased" stretch factor should be "reduced" stretch factor.
- Page 7, before the theorem: the communication complexities of the two models are given in reverse order.

Some questions:
- What are the limitations of the random uniform assumption for edge distribution? Page 6 mentions that r_e is known and the same for all sites.
- Top of Page 7: How is the communication cost of the last iteration small? Why are the selected edges only O~(n)? Don't you sample with const probability?
- Isn't Theorem 4's guarantee trivial, as the k^3 terms cancel out?
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper adapts certain types of distributed sparsification techniques to a new model, but it's not clear how much of an improvement this is. The technique does not seem novel either. There are no experiments to motivate the model or show the effectiveness of the algorithms.

content.title: Communication-Optimal Distributed Graph Clustering under Duplication Models
content.abstract: We consider the problem of clustering graph nodes over large-scale distributed graphs, when graph edges with possibly edge duplicates are observed distributively. Although edge duplicates across different sites appear to be beneficial at the first glance, in fact they could make the clustering task more complicated since potentially their processing would need extra computations and communications. We propose the first communication-optimal algorithms for two well-established communication models namely the message passing and the blackboard models. Specifically, given a graph on $n$ nodes with edges observed at $s$ sites, our algorithms achieve communication costs $\tilde{O}(ns)$ and $\tilde{O}(n+s)$ ($\tilde{O}$ hides a polylogarithmic factor), which almost match their lower bounds, $\Omega(ns)$ and $\Omega(n+s)$, in the message passing and the blackboard models respectively. The communication costs are asymptotically the same as those under non-duplication models, under a mild assumption on edge distribution. Our algorithms can also guarantee clustering quality nearly as good as that of centralizing all edges and then applying any standard clustering algorithm.
